Reading AILobbying: The Information Game

Lobbying — the direct communication by organized groups with government officials for the purpose of influencing their decisions — is the most visible and most studied form of interest group activity. The term itself derives from the lobbies of legislative chambers, where early advocates would wait to buttonhole legislators before and after floor sessions. Today, professional lobbying in Washington and state capitals is a multi-billion-dollar industry employing thousands of specialists whose knowledge of legislative procedure, regulatory process, and political relationships is the primary product they sell.

The core function of lobbying, despite its sometimes unsavory reputation in popular discourse, is fundamentally informational. Legislators and their staffs face an impossible informational challenge: they are asked to make informed decisions on hundreds of complex policy questions — ranging from agricultural subsidies to telecommunications regulation to pharmaceutical approval processes — while possessing only general expertise in any of them. Professional lobbyists, many of whom are deeply specialized in particular policy domains, fill this informational gap. They provide technical analysis of proposed legislation, explain the likely consequences of regulatory changes for the industries or groups they represent, offer draft legislative language that advances their clients' interests, and help legislators understand the political implications of various policy choices for the constituencies that care most intensely about those choices.

Word help: lobbying = talking with officials to influence their decisions · buttonhole = stop someone to talk · informational = about giving facts · specialists = experts · pharmaceutical = about medicines · draft legislative language = a first version of a bill's wording · constituencies = groups of voters or supporters · implications = effects

Chapter 13, Section III, “Strategies of Influence: Lobbying and Litigation.”

Reading AJThe Revolving Door

The close relationship between professional lobbying and the government agencies and offices that lobbyists seek to influence has produced what critics call the "revolving door" — the pattern in which government officials leave their positions to become lobbyists for the industries they previously regulated, and in which lobbyists move into government positions that give them authority over the policy areas in which they previously worked as advocates. The revolving door creates a concern about captured regulation: the possibility that regulatory agencies and legislative offices become so closely aligned with the organized interests that lobby them most intensely that they effectively serve those interests rather than the broader public. The concern is not that individual officials are corrupt — most are not — but that the structural relationships created by the revolving door skew the informational environment in which policy decisions are made, systematically privileging the perspectives of organized interests over those of the unorganized public.

Word help: revolving door = moving back and forth between government jobs and lobbying jobs · regulated = controlled by government rules · captured regulation = when an agency serves the industry it is supposed to watch · structural = built into the system · skew = tilt · privileging = giving special advantage · unorganized public = ordinary people not in a lobbying group

Chapter 13, Section III, “Lobbying: The Information Game.”

Information or influence? Use both lobbying readings. What useful thing do lobbyists provide to lawmakers? What concern does the revolving door create, and does the chapter say individual officials are corrupt?

Reading AKLitigation and Amicus Briefs

When the legislative and executive branches of government produce outcomes that interest groups cannot accept — or when groups lack the organizational strength to compete effectively in the legislative arena — the courts offer an alternative venue for pursuing policy change. Litigation, the strategic use of legal proceedings to advance policy goals, has been one of the most important and most productive strategies in the interest group toolkit, particularly for groups representing minorities, the poor, or other constituencies that face structural disadvantages in majoritarian legislative politics.

The most celebrated example of litigation as a policy strategy is the NAACP Legal Defense Fund's campaign against racial segregation, which culminated in the Supreme Court's decision in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. Unable to persuade Southern-dominated legislatures to voluntarily dismantle the Jim Crow system, and working in a Congress where Southern senators had the power to filibuster any civil rights legislation, Thurgood Marshall and the NAACP pursued a carefully constructed legal strategy that used the courts as the primary vehicle for constitutional change.

Interest groups that cannot serve as direct parties to litigation — because they do not have standing to sue in a particular case — can still participate in judicial proceedings through the filing of amicus curiae briefs, or "friend of the court" briefs. An amicus brief is a legal document filed by a third party who is not directly involved in the case but who has relevant expertise or a significant interest in its outcome, offering arguments, evidence, or perspectives that the court might not otherwise consider.

Word help: litigation = using lawsuits to reach a goal · NAACP Legal Defense Fund = the civil rights legal group led by Thurgood Marshall · segregation = forced separation by race · filibuster = a Senate tactic to block a vote by talking · standing = the legal right to bring a case · amicus curiae = “friend of the court” · perspectives = points of view

Chapter 13, Section III, “Litigation: The Courtroom as a Strategic Arena.”

Reading ALElectioneering and the PAC System

The third major strategy through which interest groups seek to influence government is electioneering — direct participation in the electoral process to help elect candidates who share the group's policy goals and to defeat those who oppose them. Electioneering can take many forms: endorsing candidates, organizing voter registration and mobilization drives, running advertising campaigns that highlight a candidate's position on the group's key issues, and most visibly, providing financial support to campaigns and political organizations.

The federal campaign finance system that existed through most of the second half of the twentieth century was built on the premise that large contributions to political candidates or parties created at least the appearance of corruption — of purchased political access — and that the government had a legitimate interest in limiting such contributions to preserve the integrity of democratic governance. The Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 and its subsequent amendments established contribution limits, disclosure requirements, and a system of public financing for presidential campaigns. These rules permitted the formation of Political Action Committees — organizations through which interest groups could collect voluntary contributions from their members and distribute those funds to supported candidates, subject to strict limits on the amount any single PAC could contribute to any single candidate.

Word help: electioneering = taking part in elections to help or defeat candidates · endorsing = publicly supporting · mobilization = getting people involved · Federal Election Campaign Act = the main law on campaign money · disclosure requirements = rules that make groups report their money · public financing = money from the government for campaigns · PAC = a group that collects money from members and gives it to candidates · integrity = honesty

Chapter 13, Section III, “Electioneering, PACs, and the Transformation of Campaign Finance.”

Reading AMCitizens United and the Super PAC

The critical turning point came with the Supreme Court's decision in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), a case that arose from a conservative nonprofit organization's desire to air a documentary film critical of Hillary Clinton during the 2008 presidential primary season. The Court, in a five-to-four decision written by Justice Anthony Kennedy, held that the First Amendment prohibits the government from restricting independent political expenditures by corporations, associations, or labor unions. The key word was "independent": the Court did not hold that corporations could contribute directly to candidates — that restriction remained in place — but it held that they could spend unlimited amounts on political advertising and communications as long as they did not coordinate those expenditures directly with a candidate's campaign.

The practical consequence of Citizens United was the rapid development of a new form of political organization — the Super PAC, or independent expenditure-only committee — that could raise unlimited sums from corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals and spend those funds on political advertising, voter outreach, and other election-related activities, subject only to the requirement of non-coordination with official campaigns. Super PACs transformed the financial landscape of American elections within a single cycle. In the 2012 election, the first full presidential election cycle after Citizens United, Super PACs spent over a billion dollars — dramatically exceeding their official campaign counterparts in total outside spending in many races. By the 2020 election cycle, outside spending by Super PACs and other independent groups had become a standard, pervasive feature of major electoral contests at every level of government.

Word help: Citizens United v. FEC = a 2010 Supreme Court decision on political spending · five-to-four = a close vote of the nine justices · independent expenditure = money spent on speech without working with a campaign · coordinate = plan together · Super PAC = a group that can raise and spend unlimited money if it does not coordinate with candidates · unions = organizations of workers · outside spending = money spent by groups other than the candidates and parties

Chapter 13, Section III, “Electioneering, PACs, and the Transformation of Campaign Finance.”

Reading ANCitizens United: Two Views

The implications of the Citizens United decision and the Super PAC era it produced are deeply contested. Supporters of the decision argue that spending money on political communication is a form of protected political speech, that restrictions on such spending inevitably favor incumbents and established interests by limiting challengers' ability to communicate their messages, and that the disclosure requirements that remain in place provide voters with the information they need to evaluate politically motivated spending. Critics argue that the practical effect of unlimited outside spending is to amplify the political voice of wealthy individuals and corporations to a degree that overwhelms the voices of ordinary citizens, that nominal non-coordination requirements are easily evaded in practice, and that the scale of Super PAC spending creates the kind of appearance of purchased political access that the pre-Citizens United campaign finance system was designed to prevent.

Word help: contested = argued over · protected speech = speech the First Amendment covers · incumbents = officials already in office · challengers = people running against incumbents · coordination = planning together · evaded = avoided in a sneaky way · amplify = make louder · appearance of purchased access = how it looks when money seems to buy meetings or votes

Chapter 13, Section III, “Electioneering, PACs, and the Transformation of Campaign Finance.”

Part 10 of 10

Make Your Argument

CORE OBJECTIVES

FQ 1: Essential Question: How are political values formed, and how does the measurement of public opinion influence the strategic behavior of government institutions?

FQ 7: Essential Question: How do political parties and interest groups serve as "linkage institutions" that connect citizens to the strategic operations of government?

FQ 11: Explain the strategies interest groups use to influence policy, including lobbying, litigation, the filing of amicus curiae briefs, and electioneering, and assess how the "revolving door" and the logic of collective action shape the effectiveness of these strategies.

IN MY WORDS: Is it fair that some groups are easier to organize than others? Why might that happen?

Reading AOThe Iron Triangle

The concept of the iron triangle describes a mutually reinforcing relationship among three institutional actors: a congressional committee or subcommittee with jurisdiction over a particular policy domain, the executive branch agencies that implement policy in that domain, and the interest groups that represent the private sector constituencies most affected by those policies. The triangular relationship is "iron" because each actor in the triangle has resources and interests that align with those of the others, creating a stable, self-reinforcing system that tends to produce policy favorable to the interests represented within the triangle and resistant to outside interference.

The congressional committee provides legislative authorization, appropriations, and oversight for the policy domain; in exchange, it receives campaign contributions from the interest groups and the political support of constituencies that benefit from favorable policy. The executive agency implements policy in ways that reflect the preferences of the interest groups it most closely interacts with; in exchange, it receives congressional support for its budget and organizational autonomy. The interest groups provide both the financial resources and the specialized expertise that sustain the other two vertices of the triangle; in exchange, they receive favorable regulatory treatment, government contracts, or policy outcomes that advance their members' interests. The system works well for its participants and tends to be highly stable — but it does so by effectively removing certain policy domains from democratic contestation, insulating them from the broader accountability processes that the constitutional system is supposed to provide.

Word help: iron triangle = a steady, mutually helpful relationship among a congressional committee, an agency, and an interest group · jurisdiction = the area where an office has authority · implements = carries out · appropriations = money Congress sets aside · oversight = watching to make sure laws are followed · autonomy = independence · contestation = debate and competition

Chapter 13, Section IV, “The Iron Triangle and Captured Policy.”

Visual PThe Iron Triangle

This diagram was made for this assignment from the chapter's description. It is an illustration, not a photograph.

What to look for: Trace each side of the triangle and read what is traded. Then find the dashed box for the public, set outside the triangle.

Diagram built from Chapter 13, Part IV description (illustration).

Reading APIssue Networks

The iron triangle framework has been criticized for overstating the stability and insularity of interest group-government relationships in many policy areas. In reality, policy domains that once appeared to be firmly controlled by stable triangular relationships have been disrupted by shifts in public opinion, the emergence of new organized interests, changes in political leadership, or external shocks that force previously settled questions back onto the active policy agenda. The concept of issue networks — developed by political scientist Hugh Heclo in the 1970s as a deliberate challenge to the iron triangle model — suggests that in most policy domains, the pattern of influence is better characterized as a fluid, porous, and constantly changing network of actors with varying degrees of commitment and expertise, rather than a stable triad of mutually reinforcing insiders.

Word help: issue networks = loose, changing groups of people who care about a policy issue · Hugh Heclo = the political scientist who developed the idea · insular = closed off from outsiders · external shocks = sudden events from outside · fluid = changing easily · porous = open, letting things in · triad = a group of three · insiders = people with special access

Chapter 13, Section IV, “The Iron Triangle and Captured Policy.”

Triangle or network? Compare the iron triangle with issue networks. Which one gives ordinary citizens a better chance to be heard, and why? Name one thing that can break a triangle open.

Reading AQFree Riders and Selective Benefits

Interest groups face a fundamental organizational challenge that political scientist Mancur Olson identified and analyzed in his landmark 1965 work, "The Logic of Collective Action." The challenge is this: many of the goods that interest groups seek from government — clean air, financial regulation, consumer protection standards, lower taxes — are what economists call public goods, meaning that once they are obtained, they are available to everyone in the relevant group regardless of whether those individuals contributed to securing them. A worker who benefits from a union's successful negotiation of higher wages and safer working conditions receives those benefits whether or not they paid union dues. A citizen who breathes cleaner air because an environmental organization successfully lobbied for stricter pollution standards receives that benefit whether or not they donated to the organization. This creates the free-rider problem: the rational individual calculus suggests that one should allow others to bear the costs of political organizing and simply collect the resulting benefits without contributing.

The organizational response to the free-rider problem has been the development of selective benefits — inducements available only to dues-paying members that give individuals a private reason to join the organization beyond their interest in the collective goods the organization pursues.

The American Association of Retired Persons offers its members discounts on insurance, travel, and retail purchases, as well as a subscription to a magazine and access to various services — benefits that are simply unavailable to non-members regardless of how much they benefit from AARP's advocacy on Social Security and Medicare.

Word help: free-rider problem = when people enjoy a benefit without helping pay for it · public goods = benefits everyone shares, like clean air · collective action = people working together for a shared goal · Mancur Olson = the economist who explained the problem in 1965 · rational = based on careful thinking about costs and benefits · union dues = fees workers pay to belong to a union · selective benefits = rewards only members get

Chapter 13, Section IV, “The Free-Rider Problem and the Logic of Collective Action.”

Why join? In your own words, explain the free-rider problem using the example of union dues or clean air. Then explain how selective benefits help a group solve it.

Reading ARThe Competitive Equilibrium of Factions

The system of political parties and interest groups, for all its imperfections, performs the fundamental function Madison identified in Federalist No. 10: it organizes the competition of factions in ways that prevent any single faction from permanently dominating the others.

Neither parties nor interest groups are perfect instruments of democratic governance, and the flaws of each have been extensively documented: the structural barriers that maintain the two-party duopoly at the expense of political diversity, the elite bias of the interest group system, the corrosive effects of unlimited campaign spending on the integrity of democratic representation. But the alternatives — a partyless democracy of uncoordinated individuals, or a factionless republic in which organized advocacy is prohibited — would create problems far worse than those the existing system produces. Parties and interest groups, whatever their limitations, are the institutional mechanisms through which a large, diverse, pluralistic democracy manages the conflict of interests that is the inevitable product of human freedom in political society.

Word help: competitive equilibrium = a balance created by competing groups · duopoly = control by two · elite bias = leaning toward the wealthy and powerful · corrosive = slowly damaging · alternatives = other choices · partyless = without parties · factionless = without organized groups · pluralistic = made up of many different groups

Chapter 13, Section IV, “The Competitive Equilibrium of Factions.”

Reading ASConclusion: Linkage Institutions in the Balance

Political parties and interest groups are, in Madison's terms, factions — organized groups pursuing particular interests in the political arena. Madison both feared them and, ultimately, relied upon them as the mechanism through which the extended republic would manage conflict and preserve liberty. Two and a quarter centuries of American political experience have borne out the essential insight of his analysis: the competition of organized interests is not the antithesis of democratic governance but one of its essential expressions. A democracy in which citizens could not organize, advocate, and compete for political influence would be a democracy in which the powerful exercised their advantages with no organized opposition and no institutional counterweight.

The transformation of campaign finance law through decisions like Citizens United represents the most significant recent challenge to the balance these institutions are supposed to maintain. When the ability of organized money to influence electoral outcomes is effectively unlimited, the linkage function of both parties and interest groups is distorted — pulled away from the preferences of ordinary citizens and toward the preferences of the small number of wealthy individuals and organizations capable of sustaining major independent expenditures. Whether the American political system can develop new norms, regulations, or institutional arrangements capable of restoring a more democratic balance within the linkage institution framework remains one of the most consequential open questions in American political life.

Word help: linkage = connection · accountability = being responsible to voters · counterweight = something that balances · constraint = limit · distorted = twisted out of shape · independent expenditures = money spent separately from a campaign · norms = shared expectations · consequential = very important

Chapter 13, Chapter Conclusion.

Source FMadison on Controlling Faction (Federalist No. 10)

James Madison, writing as “Publius” in 1787, explained why a free republic will always have factions. This is the passage the chapter uses for its Primary Source question.

“By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest ...”
“The inference to which we are brought is, that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be sought in the means of controlling its EFFECTS.”
“Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens; or if such a common motive exists, it will be more difficult for all who feel it to discover their own strength, and to act in unison with each other.”

Word help: faction = a group that pushes its own interests · actuated = driven · impulse = a sudden strong urge · inference = a conclusion · causes = what makes something happen · effects = what happens as a result · sphere = the size of a country · unison = all together at the same time
